sentences.text: This marine reptile possessed a neck measuring approximately 7.1 meters in length.
Its skeleton included 72 neck vertebrae, ranking second only to Albertonectes in total count.
The animal likely featured a slender, triangular skull similar to other members of its family.
Sharp teeth were adapted to trap and swallow prey whole rather than crushing hard shells.
A pointed snout created an aerodynamic shape that allowed for faster movement through the water.
Edward Drinker Cope named the genus Elasmosaurus in 1868 after finding the first specimen near Fort Wallace, Kansas.
The holotype, found in a ravine within the Pierre Shale formation, was redescribed in detail in 2005 by Sven Sachs.
Details about Theophilus Hunt Turner's discovery of the type specimen remained unknown until his letters were published in 1987.
The only valid species currently recognized is E. platyurus.
Discosaurus carinatus, originally described by Cope in 1868, is now considered a synonym of Elasmosaurus.
Fossils date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, roughly between 80.6 and 77 million years ago.
Remains are found in marine deposits from the Western Interior Seaway.
Scientists debate whether a fragmentary specimen from Germany belongs to the genus Elasmosaurus.

Cope initially reconstructed the animal with the skull at the tail end, a mistake corrected by Joseph Leidy. Leidy later concluded Elasmosaurus was identical to Discosaurus, a genus he named in 1851. Cope had previously believed the original material consisted of two different animals, referring to a smaller part as Discosaurus carinatus in a 1868 letter.
It is also debated whether elasmosaurids used gastroliths to aid digestion while feeding on small fish and marine invertebrates.
